newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICO'S FOX SEES PESO OVERVALUED, RATES TOO HIGH.
newsitem.headline: MEXICO'S FOX SEES PESO OVERVALUED, RATES TOO HIGH.

text.p: Vicente Fox, an opposition state governor who plans to run for the Mexican presidency in the year 2000, on Wednesday said the peso was overvalued and interest rates were too high.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Fox said the peso was eight percent overvalued, which was putting pressure on the trade balance.

Its base level to help exporters should be around 8.25/8.40 per dollar, compared with its current level of 7.78, he said. The strong peso was already causing imports to rise faster than exports, which he said was a strong signal of overvaluation.
"In this country when the signal is out that the peso is overvalued, many things happen -- earthquakes," he said, in a wry reminder of the 1994 peso crisis.

Fox, an influential member of the conservative National Action Party (PAN) who is governor of the central state of Guanajuato, was speaking after his party performed worse than expected in the July 6 elections for Chamber of Deputies.

He has urged his party to move toward the "social center" noting that winds around the world were blowing "in favor of the left." But he says he is no populist and favors privatizing Mexico's jealously-protected state oil firm Petroleos Mexicanos.
Asked how he would manage a currency slide, he said he would let the markets decide the level of interest rates as freely as they do the price of the peso.

"Financial authorities are letting free the exchange rate to the supply and demand of the market. They should do the same thing with interest rates because they keep them too high intentionally to keep attracting capital," he said.
Mexican authorities say the markets already do set interest rates and deny they meddle with them by tweaking liquidity.

Fox also said interest payments on Mexico's foreign debt were excessive and that, if he took power, he would start negotiations "with intelligent businessmen throughout the world" to extend maturities and cut foreign debt servicing.
"If we could build up a negotiation to extend the period of negotiation to a longer time, Mexico could come back to being a very strong and succesful country," he said.
He flatly ruled out a default, however.
